references.label: Hameln ceftriaxone calcium compatibility
references.citation: hameln pharma ltd. Ceftriaxone 1 g powder for solution for injection/infusion. UK SmPC §§4.2–4.5; text revised 21 April 2026, accessed 1 November 2026.
references.excerpt:
Premature neonates up to a postmenstrual age of 41 weeks (gestational age + chronological age)
Simultaneous administration of probenecid does not reduce the elimination of ceftriaxone.
references.reviewNote: Scoped compatibility/neonatal/probenecid review only. Neonates ≤28 days needing or expected to need IV calcium are contraindicated regardless of lines/timing. Older-patient sequential conditions are product-controlled. This label contains a narrow continuous-TPN paragraph; do not transfer it to B. Braun calcium gluconate or infer whole-record dose validation.

references.label: Calcium chloride compatibility SmPC
references.citation: Calcium Chloride 10% w/v Intravenous Infusion (calcium chloride dihydrate 100 mg/mL). UK SmPC §§4.4–4.5; accessed 1 November 2026.
references.excerpt: For interaction between calcium containing products and ceftriaxone, please see sections 4.4 above.
references.reviewNote: Compatibility scope only, not dose/formulation interchangeability. All-age simultaneous prohibition and >28-day sequential conditions; its continuous-TPN paragraph is not a general permission and cannot override neonatal ceftriaxone contraindications or B. Braun gluconate restrictions.

references.label: B Braun calcium gluconate compatibility
references.citation: B. Braun. Calcium Gluconate 10 % w/v Injection BP. UK SmPC §§4.3–4.5; accessed 1 November 2026.
references.excerpt: Sequential infusions of ceftriaxone and calcium-containing products must be avoided in case of hypovolaemia.
references.reviewNote: Product-specific compatibility review only: no mixing or simultaneous IV ceftriaxone/calcium even at separate lines/sites; neonatal contraindication, conditional >28-day sequential use and hypovolaemia restriction. No continuous-TPN simultaneous-use exception in this product's §§4.3–4.5.

references.label: Chastre 2003 VAP Duration
references.citation: Chastre J, Wolff M, Fagon JY, et al. Comparison of 8 vs 15 days of antibiotic therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia in adults: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2003;290(19):2588-2598.
references.excerpt: Compared with patients treated for 15 days, those treated for 8 days had neither excess mortality (18.8% vs 17.2%; difference, 1.6%; 90% confidence interval [CI], -3.7% to 6.9%) nor more recurrent infections (28.9% vs 26.0%; difference, 2.9%; 90% CI, -3.2% to 9.1%), but they had more mean (SD) antibiotic-free days (13.1 [7.4] vs 8.7 [5.2] days, P<.001).

references.label: BALANCE 2025
references.citation: BALANCE Investigators for the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group. Antibiotic treatment for 7 versus 14 days in patients with bloodstream infections. N Engl J Med. 2025 (published online 20 Nov 2024).
references.excerpt: By 90 days, 261 patients (14.5%) receiving antibiotics for 7 days had died and 286 patients (16.1%) receiving antibiotics for 14 days had died (difference, -1.6 percentage points [95.7% confidence interval {CI}, -4.0 to 0.8]), which showed the noninferiority of the shorter treatment duration.

references.label: MERINO 2018
references.citation: Harris PNA, Tambyah PA, Lye DC, et al. Effect of piperacillin-tazobactam vs meropenem on 30-day mortality for patients with E coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infection and ceftriaxone resistance: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2018;320(10):984-994.
references.excerpt: A total of 23 of 187 patients (12.3%) randomized to piperacillin-tazobactam met the primary outcome of mortality at 30 days compared with 7 of 191 (3.7%) randomized to meropenem.

references.citation: Kalil AC, Metersky ML, Klompas M, et al. Management of adults with hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia: 2016 IDSA/ATS clinical practice guidelines. Clin Infect Dis. 2016;63(5):e61-e111.

references.label: NICE NG15

references.label: Curr Opin Crit Care 2022 AMS
references.citation: Antimicrobial stewardship. Curr Opin Crit Care. 2022;28(5):551-556.
references.excerpt: AMS-interventions can improve the quality and quantity of antimicrobial prescribing in the ICU without compromising patient outcomes. The de-escalation of empiric therapy according to microbiology results and the limitation of treatment duration are important steps to reduce resistance pressure.

references.label: Drugs Today 2003 Cycling
references.citation: Cycling chemotherapy: a promising approach to reducing the morbidity and mortality of nosocomial infections. Drugs Today (Barc). 2003;39(9):697-707.
references.excerpt: There have been numerous attempts to curtail antibiotic usage through various forms of antibiotic stewardship: formulary restriction, computerized decision-support and abbreviated course empiric therapy. Cycling chemotherapy for empiric treatment of suspected infection is a method uniquely designed to address these challenges.

references.label: BMC Infect Dis 2019 cIAI
references.citation: The 2018 Lebanese Society of Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology guidelines for the use of antimicrobial therapy in complicated intra-abdominal infections in the era of antimicrobial resistance. BMC Infect Dis. 2019;19:293.
references.excerpt: Prompt and adequate antimicrobial therapy for cIAI reduces morbidity and mortality; however, the duration of therapy should be limited to no more than 4 days when adequate source control is achieved and the patient is clinically stable.

references.label: Nat Rev Microbiol 2015 (Resistance mechanisms)
references.citation: Blair JMA, Webber MA, Baylay AJ, Ogbolu DO, Piddock LJV. Molecular mechanisms of antibiotic resistance. Nature Reviews Microbiology. 2015;13(1):42-51.

references.label: SSC 2021 Antimicrobials
references.citation: Evans L et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021. Section: Antimicrobial Therapy.
references.excerpt: For adults with possible septic shock or a high likelihood for sepsis, we recommend administering antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 h of recognition. For adults with possible sepsis without shock, if concern for infection persists, we recommend administering antimicrobials within 3 h. We recommend empirical broad-spectrum therapy with one or more agents to cover all likely pathogens. We recommend daily assessment for de-escalation.

references.label: BJA Educ 2016

references.label: NICE NG253
references.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management (NG253). Published 19 November 2025; last updated 23 September 2026.
references.excerpt: Give people aged 16 or over who are at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic treatment, within 1 hour of calculating the person's NEWS2 score on initial assessment in the emergency department or on ward deterioration.

references.label: ASHP/IDSA Vancomycin 2020
references.citation: Rybak MJ, Le J, Lodise TP, et al. Therapeutic monitoring of vancomycin for serious methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infections: a revised consensus guideline and review by ASHP, IDSA, PIDS and SIDP. Am J Health Syst Pharm. 2020;77(11):835-864.
references.excerpt: We recommend an AUC/MIC ratio of 400-600 mg*hour/L (assuming a broth microdilution MIC of 1 mg/L) to achieve clinical efficacy and ensure safety for patients being treated for serious MRSA infections.
references.reviewNote: Applies to serious MRSA infection; not a universal requirement for every vancomycin course.

references.label: SSC 2026 procalcitonin
references.citation: Society of Critical Care Medicine / ESICM. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026. Antimicrobial initiation and duration. Accessed 1 November 2026.
references.excerpt: For adults with possible or probable sepsis or septic shock, we suggest using clinical evaluation alone over procalcitonin plus clinical evaluation to decide whether to start antimicrobial therapy. For adults with an initial diagnosis of sepsis or septic shock and adequate source control where optimal duration of therapy is unclear, we suggest using procalcitonin AND clinical evaluation to decide when to discontinue antimicrobial therapy over clinical evaluation alone.
references.reviewNote: Conditional recommendations: procalcitonin is an adjunct after adequate source control, not a trigger to start or a stand-alone stopping rule. NICE NG253 (2026 update) separately allows considering procalcitonin in medium- or high-risk adults alongside standard assessment; neither source supports using it alone.

cards.question: Why does volume of distribution change for hydrophilic antibiotics in sepsis?
cards.answer: Capillary leak and aggressive fluid resuscitation expand Vd for β-lactams, aminoglycosides and glycopeptides, often requiring loading doses (e.g. meropenem 2 g, vancomycin 25–30 mg/kg) to reach therapeutic levels.

cards.question: When should antibiotic infusions be used over bolus dosing?
cards.answer: Time-dependent agents (β-lactams) benefit from extended (3–4 h) or continuous infusion when MICs are high or patient is critically ill (BLING-III, MERCY trials suggest mortality benefit in severe sepsis).

cards.question: How is antibiotic de-escalation safely performed?
cards.answer: Review at 48–72 h with cultures and biomarkers (procalcitonin trend); narrow spectrum, stop empirical cover not supported by cultures, and limit duration to 5–7 days for most infections (7 days for HAP/VAP per IDSA/PneumA, and as short as 5 days if clinically improving).
